description: Am Edward a full-stack developer from zone01 Kisumu
summary:
Star Hunters is a browser-based discovery tool for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. It
lets anyone blink and subtract near-infrared sky images taken at different epochs, so
stationary stars cancel out and moving objects stand out. These include high proper
motion stars, ultra-cold brown dwarfs, comets, asteroids and variable stars. Users can
filter by wavelength across SPHEREx's six detector arrays (0.75 to 5.0 µm), click any
source to trace it across epochs, and open a 102-band spectrum with molecular bands
marked (H2O, CH4, CO2, CO). Spectra can be downloaded as CSV. A "What's above me?"
mode turns the user's location into a zenith sky patch. The backend merges Gaia, WISE
and NASA MOST catalogs into a list of known objects with per-epoch positions. Twelve
pre-computed showcase targets load instantly and are cached for slow connections. Live
sky queries are also supported. The tool matters because multi-epoch infrared surveys
are hard to explore without specialist software. Star Hunters makes the same workflow
visual and fast for both enthusiasts and researchers.
details:
• What it does:
    • Blink or subtract two epochs, with a wavelength range slider.
    • Click-to-track moving sources across epochs, with a per-epoch waypoint table, proper motion, and a catalog match or an “uncataloged infrared mover candidate” flag.
    • Known-object checklist with fuzzy search, Check All / Uncheck All, and one-click tracking.
    • 102-channel spectrum viewer with uncertainty ribbons per detector and CSV export.
    • Guided tour of 12 showcase targets: WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, R Draconis, Comet 3I/ATLAS, Luhman 16, Wolf 359, Teegarden’s Star, CW Leonis, T Tauri and Ceres.
    • A FastAPI backend queries the IRSA archive for SPHEREx and WISE, cross-matches WISE against Gaia within 2.5 arcsec, and propagates proper motions to each epoch.
    • It streams the images as binary Float16/Float32 frames and caches them in SQLite.
    • The React and TypeScript frontend draws them on canvas, with two-tier client caching for 3G-friendly use.
  • Impact: it lowers the barrier to spotting movers in multi-epoch infrared data and gives researchers a quick spectrum view.
  • Tools: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Astropy, Astroquery, SQLite, React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Docker and Fly.io.
  • Creative angle: the zenith-based discovery flow, the molecular-band shading, and the offline-first design.
  • Design factors: low bandwidth, clutter control by auto-checking only notable movers, and accessibility.
